description:
## The warnings are legitimate

Every `type/no-matching-clause` warning the runtime library emits is correct, and the smallest case shows why:

```
fn f([]), do: 0
fn f([_h | _t]), do: 1
```

warns. A reader sees an exhaustive match -- every list is empty or a cons -- but the parameter has no declared domain, so it is `any`, and `f(:atom)` really does match no clause and really would halt with `:function_clause`.

Declaring the domain silences it completely:

```
@spec f([a]) :: integer
fn f([]), do: 0
fn f([_h | _t]), do: 1
```

Zero warnings. The compiler was right both times.

## The correlation is exact

Every warned helper in `lib/enum.fz` has no `@spec`: `map_list`, `filter_list`, `flat_map_list`, `map_reduce_list`, `scan_first`, `scan_list`, `intersperse_list`, `intersperse_tail`, `map_join_list`, `map_join_tail`, `map_intersperse_list`, `map_intersperse_tail`. The helpers beside them that do carry one -- `with_index_list`, `reverse_list`, `map_every_list` -- do not warn.

The same holds in `lib/json.fz` and `lib/map.fz`: `decode_done`, `elements`, `escape`, `fraction`, `pairs`, `reverse` all warn and all lack a spec.

## What to do

Declare the domains. This is not warning suppression -- an undeclared parameter genuinely admits values the clauses do not handle, and writing the spec is what makes the function total rather than what hides that it is not.

`Json.encode!/1` is the one exception and needs deciding separately: it declares `@spec encode!(any) :: binary` and its domain really is wider than its clauses, since `any` includes tuples and pids it cannot encode. Either the spec narrows to what JSON can represent, or a final clause says what happens to the rest.

## Acceptance

- Every private helper in the runtime library declares its parameter and result types.
- The library compiles with no `type/no-matching-clause` warning, or each surviving one names a function whose domain is genuinely wider than its clauses.
- The fixture diagnostics goldens shrink accordingly.
title: The runtime library's clause-coverage warnings are all missing domain declarations
